For $$\left[\mathrm{FeCl}_4\right]^{-}$$

In this complex,

$$\mathrm{Fe}$$ is in +3 oxidation state and $$\mathrm{CN}^{-}$$ is a strong field ligand. So, pairing of electron will takes place.

en.explanation:
$$\begin{aligned} \text { Given, } m_1 & =100 \mathrm{~g} \\ V_1 & =V_1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ m_2 & =50 \mathrm{~g} \\ V_2 & =1.5 V_1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

$$\frac{\lambda\left(m_1\right)}{\lambda\left(m_2\right)}=?$$

Using the formula of de-Broglie's wavelength, we will get

$$\lambda=\frac{h}{m v}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{m_2 V_2}{m_1 V_1}=\frac{50 \times 1.5 V_1}{100 V_1}=\frac{3}{4}$$

So, the ratio is 3 : 4.

First order with respect to both A and B.
First order with respect to A and second order with respect to B.
Second order with respect to A and first order with respect to B.

en.explanation:
For the given reaction, $$A+B \rightarrow C$$, rate equation is given by

$$R=k[A]^x[B]^y$$

where, $$x$$ and $$y$$ are the orders w.r.t. $$A$$ and $$B$$ respectively. So, from the given data we can write

$$\begin{aligned} 100 & =k[1]^x[10]^y \quad \text{.... (i)}\\ 1 & =k[1]^x[1]^y \quad \text{.... (ii)}\\ 10 & =k[10]^x[1]^y \quad \text{.... (iii)} \end{aligned}$$

On dividng Eq. (ii) by Eq. (i), we will get

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{100} & =\frac{k[1]^x[1]^y}{k[1]^x[10]^y} \\ \frac{1}{100} & =\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^y \\ \Rightarrow \quad y & =2 \end{aligned}$$

Now, dividing Eq. (iii) by Eq. (ii), we will get

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{10}{1} & =\frac{k[10]^x[1]^y}{k[1]^x[1]^y} \\ 10 & =(10)^x \\ \Rightarrow \quad &x=1\end{aligned}$$

So, the reaction is 2nd order w.r.t. $$B$$ and 1st order w.r.t. $$A$$.

$$\begin{array}{l} \text { Also, } & P\left(A^{\prime} \cap B^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow & P(\overline{A \cup B})=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow & 1-P(A \cup B)=\frac{1}{2} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & \quad P(A \cup B)=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow & \quad P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad P(A)+P(B)-\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{2} \quad \text { [Using Eq. (i)] }$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad P(A)+P(B)=\frac{7}{12}$$ ..... (ii)

Now, from Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$P(A)\left\{\frac{7}{12}-P(A)\right\}=\frac{1}{12}$$

$$\begin{array}{lr} \Rightarrow & \frac{7}{12} P(A)-P(A)^2=\frac{1}{12} \\ \Rightarrow & P(A)^2-\frac{7}{12} P(A)+\frac{1}{12}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 12 P(A)^2-7 P(A)+1=0 \\ \Rightarrow & (3 P(A)-1)(4 P(A)-1)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & P(A)=\frac{1}{3} \text { or } P(A)=\frac{1}{4} \end{array}$$

en.content: The average ordinate of $$y = \sin x$$ over $$[0,\pi ]$$ is :
en.explanation:
The average value of a function $f(x)$ over an interval $[a, b]$ is given by the formula:

$$\text{Average} = \frac{1}{b - a}\int\limits_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx$$

In this case, we want to find the average value of the function $y = \sin(x)$ over the interval $[0, \pi]$. We can use the formula above, with $f(x) = \sin(x)$, $a = 0$, and $b = \pi$ :

$$\text{Average} = \frac{1}{\pi - 0}\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \sin(x) \, dx$$

The integral of $\sin(x)$ from $0$ to $\pi$ is $- \cos(\pi) + \cos(0) = -(-1) + 1 = 2$.

So, the average value is :

$$\text{Average} = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot 2 = \frac{2}{\pi}$$

So, the correct answer is Option A, $\frac{2}{\pi}$.

$$b<\mathrm{GM}$$ of $$a, b, c$$

So, $$\frac{2 a c}{a+c}$$ can be equal to $$b$$.

Hence, a, b and c can't be in AP or GP, but can be in HP.

But $$(a, c)$$ may or may not be in $$R \cup R^{\prime}$$

$$\therefore R \cup R^{\prime}$$ may or may nor be transitive.

$$R \cap R^{\prime}$$ and $$R \cup R^{\prime}$$ are also equivalence relation.

Now, substitute it in Eq. (i),

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =\int_a^0 f(x) d x+\int_0^T f(x) d x+\int_0^a f(x) d x \\ & =\int_a^0 f(x) d x+\int_0^T f(x) d x-\int_a^0 f(x) d x \\ & =\int_0^T f(x) d x, \text { which is independent on } a . \end{aligned}$$

$$f(T)=0$$ and $$f(T+(-T)=f(0)=1 \neq f(T)$$

So, $$T$$ cannot be an irrational number

Let $$T$$ is a rational number then

$$f(x+T)=f(x)=1$$, if $$x$$ is rational

$$f(x+T)=f(x)=0$$, if $$x$$ is irrational

So, $$T$$ must be rational for $$f(x)$$ a periodic function.

For Lens $$L_1 \quad u=-\frac{f}{2}, f=+f$$

$$\therefore \quad \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{-\frac{f}{2}}=\frac{1}{f}$$

$$\therefore \quad v=-f$$ and $$m=v / u=2$$

For Lens $$L_2 \quad u=-2 f, v=2 f$$

$$\therefore \quad m=\frac{v}{u}=-1$$

For Lens $$L_3 \quad u=+f, f=+f$$

$$\therefore \quad \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow v=\frac{f}{2}$$

and $$\quad m=\frac{v}{u}=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$\therefore \quad m=m_1 \cdot m_2 \cdot m_3=2 \times(-1) \times \frac{1}{2}=-1$$

Hence, final image will be $$\frac{f}{2}$$ behind the lens $$L_3$$ and the magnification is $$-$$1.

en.explanation:
$$r_{\perp}=H_{\max }=\frac{u^2 \sin ^2 \theta}{2 g}, v=u \cos \theta$$

Angular momentum at the maximum height about point $$O$$ is

$$\begin{aligned} L & =m v r_{\perp}=m(u \cos \theta)\left(\frac{u^2 \sin ^2 \theta}{2 g}\right) \\ \therefore \quad L & =\left(\frac{m u^3}{2 g}\right) \cdot \sin ^2 \theta \cos \theta \end{aligned}$$

As, $$\sin ^2 \theta$$ varies from 0 to 1 between 0 to $$\pi / 2$$.

$$\cos \theta$$ varies from 1 to 0 between 0 to $$\pi / 2$$.

$$\therefore \sin ^2 \theta \cdot \cos \theta$$ varies from 0 to 0 between 0 to $$\pi / 2$$.

At $$\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}, \sin ^2 \theta \cdot \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}$$

Given,

$$\begin{aligned} & m=2 \mathrm{~kg}, r=5 \mathrm{~m}, v=2 \sqrt{5} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & a_t=\frac{d v}{d t}=3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore$$ Centripetal acceleration or radial acceleration is

$$a_r=\frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{(2 \sqrt{5})^2}{5}=4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$$

$$\therefore$$ Net acceleration, $$a=\sqrt{a_t^2+a_r^2}$$

$$\therefore \quad a=\sqrt{(3)^2+(4)^2}=5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$$

$$\therefore$$ The force action on the body is

$$F=m a=2 \times 5=10 \mathrm{~N}$$

en.content: Acceleration due to gravity at a height H from the surface of a planet is the same as that at a depth of H below the surface. If R be the radius of the planet, then H vs. R graph for different planets will be,
en.explanation:
The acceleration due to gravity at height $$H$$ from the surface of planet is

$$g_H=\frac{G M}{(R+H)^2}$$ ..... (i)

The acceleration due to gravity at depth $$H$$ below the surface of planet is

$$g_H=\frac{G M}{R^3}(R-H)$$ .... (ii)

From Eq. (i) and (ii), we get

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{G M}{(R+H)^2}=\frac{G M}{R^3}(R-H) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad H^2+H R-R^2=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad H=\frac{-R \pm \sqrt{R^2-4 \times 1 \times\left(-R^2\right)}}{2 \times 1} \\ & =\frac{-R \pm \sqrt{5} R}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad H=\left(\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) R \\ & \Rightarrow \quad H \propto R \\ \end{aligned}$$

Hence, $$H$$ vs $$R$$ graph is straight line.

en.content: The displacement of a plane progressive wave in a medium, travelling towards positive x-axis with velocity 4 m/s at t = 0 is given by $$y = 3\sin 2\pi \left( { - {x \over 3}} \right)$$. Then the expression for the displacement at a later time t = 4 sec will be
en.explanation:
1. The general equation of a wave propagating in one dimension can be expressed as $y = A \sin(\omega t - kx + \phi)$, where $A$ is the amplitude, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $k$ is the wave number, $x$ is the position, $t$ is the time, and $\phi$ is the phase constant.

2. The given wave equation is $$y = 3\sin 2\pi \left( { - {x \over 3}} \right)$$. This can be re-written as $y = 3\sin(-2\pi {x \over 3})$, which matches the form $y = A \sin(\omega t - kx)$ where $\omega t$ is zero (i.e., $t=0$), $A$ is 3 and $k$ is $-{2\pi \over 3}$.

3. The negative sign of $k$ indicates that the wave is moving in the negative x-direction, but the problem states that the wave is moving in the positive x-direction. Hence, we should take $k$ as positive, i.e., $k = {2\pi \over 3}$.

4. The speed of the wave $v$ is given by $v = \frac{\omega}{k}$. From the problem, we know that $v = 4$ m/s. By substituting these values, we can solve for $\omega$: $4=\frac{\omega}{2 \pi / 3}$ which gives $\omega = {8\pi \over 3}$.

5. So, the wave equation at any time $t$ can be written as $y = 3 \sin \left[\frac{8 \pi}{3} t-\frac{2 \pi}{3} x\right]$.

6. Now, we want to find the wave equation at $t=4$ s. Substituting $t=4$ into the equation gives $y = 3 \sin \left[\frac{8 \pi}{3} \times 4-\frac{2 \pi}{3} x\right]$.

7. Simplifying the argument of the sine function, we get $y = 3 \sin 2 \pi\left(\frac{-x+16}{3}\right)$.

8. Rearranging the argument of the sine function again, we get $$y = 3\sin 2\pi \left( { - {x-16 \over 3}} \right)$$.

en.content: The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave of wave number k and angular frequency $$\omega$$ is given $$\vec{E}=E_{0}(\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \sin (k z-\omega t)$$. Which of the following gives the direction of the associated magnetic field $$\vec{B}$$ ?
en.explanation:
The direction of the magnetic field in an electromagnetic wave can be determined using the cross product of the wave vector and the electric field vector. In this case, the electric field is given by $\vec{E} = E_0(\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \sin(kz - \omega t)$, and the wave is propagating in the $+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ direction (along the z-axis).

The direction of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ can be found using the right-hand rule for the cross product $\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \vec{E}$, where $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ is the direction of wave propagation. In this case, $\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \hat{\mathbf{k}}$. So, we calculate :

$ \hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \vec{E} = \hat{\mathbf{k}} \times (\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}) $

This cross product gives us the direction of the magnetic field :

  • The cross product $\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}}$ yields $+\hat{\mathbf{j}}$.
  • The cross product $\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ yields $-\hat{\mathbf{i}}$.

So, combining these results, we get :

$ \hat{\mathbf{k}} \times (\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}) = -\hat{\mathbf{j}} + \hat{\mathbf{i}} = -\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}} $

Therefore, the direction of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ associated with the electromagnetic wave is $-\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}}$, which corresponds to Option B.

en.explanation:
Given, gravitational potential,

$$V=-\frac{G M}{r}+\frac{A}{r^2}$$

By principle of homogeneity,

$$\begin{aligned} {\left[\frac{G M}{r}\right] } & =\left[\frac{A}{r^2}\right] \\ \therefore \quad[A] & =[G M r] \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \text { Now, }[G]=\left[\frac{F r^2}{m_1 m_2}\right]=\frac{\left[M L T^{-2}\right]\left[\mathrm{L}^2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{M}^2\right]}=\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \cdot \mathrm{T}^{-2}\right] \\ & \therefore \quad[A]=\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-2]}[\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{L}]=\left[\mathrm{L}^4 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]\right. \end{aligned}$$

According to the question,

$$\begin{gathered} {[A]=[G]^x[M]^y[c]^z} \\ \Rightarrow\left[\mathrm{L}^4 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]=\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]^x[M]^y\left[\mathrm{LT}^{-1}\right]^z \end{gathered}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore-x+y & =0 \Rightarrow x=y \quad \text{... (i)}\\ 3 x+z & =4 \quad \text{... (ii)}\\ -2 x-z & =-2 \quad \text{... (iii)} \end{aligned}$$

From Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get

$$\begin{aligned} & x=y=2, z=-2 \\ \therefore \quad & A=G^2 M^2 c^{-2}=\frac{G^2 M^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A train is moving along the tracks at a constant speed u. A girl on the train throws a ball of mass m straight ahead along the direction of motion of the train with speed $$\mathrm{v}$$ with respect to herself. Then

options.content: Kinetic energy of the ball as measured by the girl on the train is $$\mathrm{mv}^{2} / 2$$.
Work done by the girl in throwing the ball is $$ \mathrm{mv}^{2} / 2$$.
Work done by the train is mvu.
The gain in kinetic energy of the ball as measured by a person standing by the rail track is $$\mathrm{mv}^{2} / 2$$.

en.explanation:
1. Train Frame (the frame of reference of the girl on the train) :

- The initial velocity of the ball is 0 (it's at rest before she throws it).

- The final velocity of the ball is v (after she throws it).

- So the kinetic energy (K.E.) of the ball in the train frame, after she throws it, is $$\frac{1}{2}mv^2$$.

- The work done by the girl is equal to the change in kinetic energy, so it's also $$\frac{1}{2}mv^2$$.

2. Ground Frame (the frame of reference of a person standing by the track) :

- The initial velocity of the ball is u (equal to the speed of the train, as the ball is at rest relative to the train before she throws it).

- The final velocity of the ball is u + v (the speed of the train plus the speed of the ball relative to the train).

- So, the kinetic energy (K.E.) of the ball in the ground frame, after she throws it, is $$\frac{1}{2}m(u+v)^2 = \frac{1}{2}mu^2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2 +muv$$.

- The gain in K.E. of the ball as measured by a person standing on the ground is the final K.E. minus the initial K.E., which is $$\frac{1}{2}mu^2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + muv - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + muv$$. This corresponds to the work done by the girl plus the work done by the train.

So, in conclusion:

- Option A is correct.

- Option B is correct.

- Option C is correct.

- Option D is incorrect because it's missing the term for the work done by the train (muv).

en.explanation:
Initially switch $$K$$ is closed,

Energy stored in capacitor $$A, E_A=\frac{1}{2} C V^2$$

Energy stored in capacitor $$B, E_B=\frac{1}{2} C V^2$$

$$\therefore$$ Total energy stored in two capacitors,

$$E_i=E_A+E_B=\frac{1}{2} C V^2+\frac{1}{2} C V^2=C V^2$$

When switch $$K$$ is open, and a dielectric $$(K=3)$$ is inserted in both capacitors, then

Energy stored in capacitor $$A$$,

$$E_A=\frac{1}{2}(3 C) V^2=\frac{3}{2} C V^2$$

Energy stored in capacitor B,

$$E_p=\frac{(C V)^2}{2 \times 3 C}=\frac{1}{6} C V^2$$

$$\therefore$$ Total energy stored in two capacitors,

$$E_f=E_A+E_B=\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{6}\right) C V^2=\frac{5}{3} C V^2$$

By Maxwell's equation,

For $$r < R$$,

$$\begin{aligned} & & \oint E_{\text {ind }} \cdot d l & =\frac{d \phi_B}{d t}=-\left(\frac{d B}{d t}\right) A \\ \Rightarrow & & E_{\text {ind }}(2 \pi r) & =-(8 t-2) \cdot \pi R^2 \\ \therefore & & E_{\text {ind }} & =-(4 t-1) \cdot \frac{R^2}{r} \end{aligned}$$

$$\Rightarrow E_{\text {ind }} \propto \frac{1}{r} \Rightarrow E_{\text {ind }}$$ vs $$r$$ does not vary linearly.

As $$E_{\text {ind }}$$ is a non-conservative field. So, it will form a closed loop.

Now, $$\left(\frac{d B}{d t}\right)_{t=0}=8 \times 0-2=-2$$

$$\therefore B$$ will decrease. So, by Lenz's law the charge particle will move in anti-clockwise direction to oppose the decreasing magnetic field.

$$\text { Now, }\left|E_{\text {ind }}\right|_{t=2 \mathrm{~s}}=\left.(4 t-1) \cdot \frac{R^2}{2 R}\right|_{t=2}=\frac{7 R}{2}$$

$$\therefore$$ Acceleration of charge particle is

$$a=\frac{q E_{\text {ind }}}{m}=\frac{q}{m} \cdot \frac{7 R}{2}=\frac{7 q R}{2 m}$$
